episodes.title: Leaving the Jehovah’s Witnesses: Religious Trauma & Finding Yourself Again | Elizabeth Hill
episodes.description:
What happens when the belief system that shaped your entire world no longer fits?

In this first episode of The Reconstructing, host Katie Grace sits down with Elizabeth B. Hill, author, coach, and founder of Green Heart Living Press, to explore her experience growing up as a Jehovah’s Witness, leaving a high-control religion, and rebuilding her sense of identity, spirituality, and self-worth.

Elizabeth shares how fear shaped her childhood, how leaving the religion upended her sense of self, and how decades of healing helped her rediscover her voice, reconnect with her spirituality, and find work that truly aligns with who she is. Together, Katie and Elizabeth explore religious trauma, the lasting effects of high-control environments, and the ongoing process of learning who we are beyond the beliefs and expectations we inherited.

Because leaving a belief system is only the beginning. What comes next is the work of reconstructing a life that feels like your own.

episodes.title: What Makes a Cult? Religious Trauma, Coercive Control & Rebuilding Self-Trust | Elise Heerde
episodes.description:
What makes a group a cult? How can you recognize religious trauma and coercive control when they're disguised as love, faith, protection, or belonging? And how do you learn to trust yourself again after years of being told what to believe, how to live, and who to be?

In Episode 3 of The Reconstructing, host Katie Grace sits down with Elise Heerde, a mental health practitioner, certified coach, author of "Holy Hell, Saved So Hard I Needed Therapy", and co-founder of Religious Trauma and Cults. Drawing on her own experience in high-control Pentecostal Christianity and her professional work supporting survivors, Elise explores the complicated process of recognizing harm, leaving controlling environments, and rebuilding a life beyond fear.

Together, Katie and Elise unpack what distinguishes a cult or high-control group from a religious environment that may cause harm. Elise explains why beliefs alone aren't the defining factor— and why it's more useful to examine patterns of coercive control, including isolation, monitoring, regulation of everyday life, and punishment for stepping out of line. They also discuss why harmful control can exist within seemingly mainstream religious communities, why survivors get to choose the language that best describes their own experiences, and why no one should have to prove that their trauma was “bad enough” to deserve support.

Elise offers practical guidance for rebuilding self-trust through curiosity, compassion, and small, low-stakes decisions. She explains why your nervous system may continue responding with fear or urgency even after your beliefs have changed, how to make room for uncertainty without rushing toward new answers, and why emotions can be treated as information rather than something to suppress or judge.

episodes.title: What is Religious Trauma, CPTSD & Healing After High-Control Religion | Dr. Laura E. Anderson
episodes.description:
What is religious trauma, how does it affect us, and what does healing actually look like?

In Episode 2 of The Reconstructing, host Katie Grace sits down with Dr. Laura E. Anderson, co-founder of the Religious Trauma Institute and founder of the Center for Trauma Resolution and Recovery, to explore the lasting effects of high-control religion and the process of healing from religious trauma.

Drawing from her personal experience growing up in evangelical Christianity and her professional work supporting trauma survivors, Dr. Laura breaks down the differences between adverse religious experiences, religious trauma, PTSD, and complex PTSD (CPTSD). She explains how prolonged fear and control can shape our nervous systems, identities, relationships, and sense of safety— and why symptoms sometimes become more noticeable after we begin to leave those environments.

Together, Katie and Dr. Laura explore why intellectual deconstruction alone may not resolve the effects of trauma, the importance of approaches that address both the brain and body, and how grief is an essential part of recognizing what we lost, what we needed, and who we had to become to survive.

Most importantly, Dr. Laura reminds us that healing doesn't require abandoning our faith, adopting someone else's beliefs, or rushing to figure everything out. It asks us to move slowly, build a sense of safety, reconnect with our own autonomy, and make room for joy along the way.

Note: this conversation is educational and isn't a substitute for individualized mental health care.

*Connect with Dr. Laura Anderson:

You don't have to untangle everything today. You have time to heal, to grieve, to explore, and to build a life that feels like your own.
